messages.author: 8288aa34e2f200a2
messages.subject: circular parameter
parts:
Hi Stan users,

I would like to ask about estimating a parameter that for a circular quantity (e.g. time).

I have included a toy dataset/models in the attached file that runs in r.

I am trying to model some oscillating time series data - e.g. y[i,j] ~ normal(sin(time[I,[j]+pos[j]), sigma)
Different subjects have different phase shifts (pos[j]) in the range -pi to pi
I would like to estimate the phase shift parameter.

Initially I used a uniform prior over the range -pi to pi for offset (model 1 in attached file). This resulted in the posterior distributions of pos[j] near -pi or pi being poorly estimated, presumably as the optimization method has difficulties moving between -pi and pi.

Then I tried a von meis prior with a very small kappa (0 is not allowed) for offset (model 2 in attached file). The results were similar to model 1.

Then I tried using 2 parameters with uniform prior over the range -1 to 1 (model 3, xpos and ypos). I then took the atan of ypos/xpos to get the angle. Since there are multiple values of xpos and ypos that give the same angle, I set parameter sigma to be equal to sqrt(xpos^2+ypos^2)+0.1 , to make xpos and ypos identifiable. The seemed to work better than models 1 or 2, but had the disadvantage that each individual now had their own sigma.

By chance I noticed that if I neglected to index sigma in the likleyhood function (line 241, model 4), then the estimates for the angle were more precise . Whilst the print of the model indicated there were  still as many sigma as individuals, they were now all of the same value.

My questions are
- the way I used to estimate the offset/angle in model 3 or 4 seemed better than in model 1 or 2, but I could not find examples of others doing this, so I was unsure if this is a reasonable way to do it?

- What is going on in model 4 vs model 3? I would  have expected not indexing sigma to result in an error?

Thanks for any advice you may have

Hugh










Please see the attached modell/data  file.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] circular parameter
parts:
There's a large literature on circular statistics.

We'll finally have a working version of unit vector
parameters in Stan 2.10 (out soon). And I wrote up a new
chapter for the manual (warning---I had to learn as I
went, never having done circular stats). I'm attaching
it prior to release (comments welcome, as always).

Your diagnosis is accurate --- the sampler can't move
between -pi and pi if you treat it as a line. Stan uses
an auxiliary variable parameterization somewhat like yours
(but unconstrained), and a unit normal regulaization
described in the attached chapter; there aren't any free
parameters in that, though --- you just need to fix the
scale.

If you did this

for (n in 1:N)
y[n] ~ normal(mu[n], sigma);

and sigma is an N-vector, then it's equivalent to this

for (n in 1:N)
for (m in 1:N)
y[n] ~ normal(mu[n], sigma[m]);

which is not what you want to do. It artificially multiplies
data size by N and ties all the parameters sigma[n] together.

- Bob

Thanks Bob,

I read the manual bit you sent which was most helpful. I changed the parameterization I was using based on what is in the manual, and used unit normal priors. It worked much better, but I got some divergent transitions (model 7 in the attached). I tried reducing the standard deviation of the unit normal priors and this reduced the number of divergent transitions (model 8 in attached). Reducing the SD further just made the posterior distributions more uniform (model 9).

Any thoughts on why I get the divergent transitions, and why there are less when I reduce the SD of the normal priors?

Best wishes

Hugh

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] circular parameter
parts:
The program looks OK, but maybe Michael will have some
clue.

You could start by trying to put a prior on sigma.

If you're in R, there are ways to see what the
divergences are graphically (but I can never remember what
they are).

Some efficiency tips:

You can replace ((x^2)+(y^2))^0.5 with hypot(x, y).

I don't think you have to worry about

if (x_t==0&&y_t==1) {ans <- 0.5;} // to avoid div by 0
if (x_t==0&&y_t==-1) {ans <- 1;} // to avoid div by 0

unless you'r initializing at 0, because those are measure-0
points. I'd also recommend some space around operators and in between
curly braces, as well as consistent indentation. You can
replace this:

for(h in 1:H) {
xpos[h] ~ normal(0,1);
ypos[h] ~ normal(0,1);
}

with

xpos ~ normal(0, 1);
ypos ~ normal(0, 1);

It's much more efficient.

We'll soon have the unit_vector data structure built in and
also have sin() vectorized so the likelihood can be easily
vectorized.

- Bob

parts:
Yeah, I know. I think the constraining transformation is
obfuscating the source of the divergences.

On Apr 25, 2016, at 8:15 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> They're the bright blue dots in the pairs() plots.
>
> They look like they're all over the posterior here, which
> hasn't been the case with other examples I've seen, where
> they tend to clump near boundaries.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Apr 25, 2016, at 3:08 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

>> I think you’re going to need to dump to a diagnostic file to get

>> the divergences arise.
>>

>>> in.
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>

>>>>
>>>> Hi Bob,
>>>>
>>>> Thanks for your suggestions. I put a prior on sigma, and made the efficiency changes. Still getting divergent transitions, even if I increase adapt_delta to 0.99.
>>>> Below is the pairs plot with the first and second subjects parameters and sigma. I note the x and y variables are correlated as one would expect, since the ratio stays the same as they increase multiplicatively. Do you think that could be causing the sampling problems?
>>>>
>>>> Best wishes
>>>>
>>>> Hugh
>>>> <Auto Generated Inline Image 1.png>
>>>> <Auto Generated Inline Image 2.png>
>>>> On Monday, April 25, 2016 at 1:02:38 AM UTC+7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> The program looks OK, but maybe Michael will have some
>>>> clue.
>>>>
>>>> You could start by trying to put a prior on sigma.
>>>>
>>>> If you're in R, there are ways to see what the
>>>> divergences are graphically (but I can never remember what
>>>> they are).
>>>>
>>>> Some efficiency tips:
>>>>
>>>> You can replace ((x^2)+(y^2))^0.5 with hypot(x, y).
>>>>
>>>> I don't think you have to worry about
>>>>
>>>> if (x_t==0&&y_t==1) {ans <- 0.5;} // to avoid div by 0
>>>> if (x_t==0&&y_t==-1) {ans <- 1;} // to avoid div by 0
>>>>
>>>> unless you'r initializing at 0, because those are measure-0
>>>> points. I'd also recommend some space around operators and in between
>>>> curly braces, as well as consistent indentation. You can
>>>> replace this:
>>>>
>>>> for(h in 1:H) {
>>>> xpos[h] ~ normal(0,1);
>>>> ypos[h] ~ normal(0,1);
>>>> }
>>>>
>>>> with
>>>>
>>>> xpos ~ normal(0, 1);
>>>> ypos ~ normal(0, 1);
>>>>
>>>> It's much more efficient.
>>>>
>>>> We'll soon have the unit_vector data structure built in and
>>>> also have sin() vectorized so the likelihood can be easily
>>>> vectorized.
>>>>
>>>> - Bob
